explanations.explanation: That's exactly what the text says: "For God had blessed Obed-edom." (1 Chronicles 26:5) Eight sons, and the passage hands the credit straight to God. I think that's a full house, and I can barely keep one bakery stocked.

explanations.answer: He had served the king well
explanations.explanation: The passage never gives that as the reason. After listing Obed-edom's eight sons, it says, "For God had blessed Obed-edom." (1 Chronicles 26:5) So the reason is God's blessing, and the text puts it right there.

Nothing in these verses calls Obed-edom the chief Levite. He's one of the gatekeepers, and the reason given for his eight sons is simple: "For God had blessed Obed-edom." (1 Chronicles 26:5) Sometimes the answer is sitting in the very next sentence, friend.

Yes, friend! The text says Shemaiah's sons "…ruled over their families because they were strong, capable men." (1 Chronicles 26:6) Strong and capable, and that's the reason given. Nice reading, baker.

Money never comes up in this verse. The text says they ruled over their families "…because they were strong, capable men." (1 Chronicles 26:6) Being capable is what counts here, and a full pocket doesn't get a mention.

Good guess, since it sounds like a ruling-family word. But the verse says they "…ruled over their families because they were strong, capable men." (1 Chronicles 26:6) The word is capable, and that's the reason the verse gives.

That's right. The text says Shimri wasn't the firstborn, "…his father had appointed him as the first…" (1 Chronicles 26:10) Hosah made the call himself. Shimri got the first spot on the list because of his dad's choice.

It's actually true. The text says, "although he was not the firstborn, his father had appointed him as the first…" (1 Chronicles 26:10) So Shimri's spot at the top of the list came from his father's choice, and birth order had nothing to do with it.

explanations.answer: They cast lots for each gate
explanations.explanation: Yes! "They cast lots for each gate, according to their families, young and old alike." (1 Chronicles 26:13) Every gate got its keeper by lot. Families, young and old alike, all got in on it. I think that kept everybody from arguing over the good spots.
A king is a natural guess, friend. But for the gates, the text says, "They cast lots for each gate, according to their families, young and old alike." (1 Chronicles 26:13) The lots decided it.

The priests don't pick the gates in this passage. The text says the gatekeepers "…cast lots for each gate, according to their families, young and old alike." (1 Chronicles 26:13) So the lots made the choice.
Not quite, friend. The text says the lots were cast "…according to their families, young and old alike." (1 Chronicles 26:13) So the young are in it too, not only the oldest.
That's right. The gatekeepers cast lots "…according to their families, young and old alike." (1 Chronicles 26:13) Young and old both got a turn. I think that's the fairest way to hand out a job.
That's the one! The text calls Zechariah "…a wise counselor…" and the lot for the North Gate fell to him. (1 Chronicles 26:14) A man like that at the gate sounds like a good person to have around.
Plenty of people in this chapter are called strong, so I get it. But for Zechariah, the text says "…a wise counselor…" (1 Chronicles 26:14) He was known for his wisdom.
No music for Zechariah in this verse. The text calls him "…a wise counselor…" and the North Gate went to him. (1 Chronicles 26:14) The word there is counselor, not musician.

Right! "The lot for the South Gate fell to Obed-edom, and the lot for the storehouses to his sons." (1 Chronicles 26:15) Dad got the gate and the sons got the storehouses. Sounds like a family business to me. Somebody get that family matching aprons.
No altar in this list, friend. The lot gave Obed-edom's sons "the storehouses." (1 Chronicles 26:15) Dad got the South Gate and the sons got the storehouses.
Music isn't what the lot gave them here. The verse says, "…the lot for the storehouses to his sons." (1 Chronicles 26:15) These were guard posts, not a stage.
That's the one. The text says, "There were guards stationed at every watch." (1 Chronicles 26:16) Every single watch gets a guard. I'd be the guy asking where the break room is.
The text doesn't limit the guards to feast days. It says, "There were guards stationed at every watch." (1 Chronicles 26:16) That's a much bigger commitment than a few special days.

Night guards make sense, but that isn't what it says. The text says, "There were guards stationed at every watch." (1 Chronicles 26:16) Every watch is the wording, and it doesn't pick out only the night.

Yes, friend. The text sums up the list: "These were the divisions of the gatekeepers who were descendants of Korah and Merari." (1 Chronicles 26:19) Korah and Merari, the two family lines behind all those gate posts. Nice work holding onto that whole list.

Ooh, I see the doubt, but this one is true. The text wraps up the whole list: "These were the divisions of the gatekeepers who were descendants of Korah and Merari." (1 Chronicles 26:19) That's a whole lot of names, and the verse ties them to just two: Korah and Merari.

Yes! "Now their fellow Levites were in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things." (1 Chronicles 26:20) The gates had their guards, and the treasuries had their own keepers. Different jobs, same house. Me, I can barely guard one cookie jar.

Sacrifices is a fair guess for a house of God, friend, and I'd have said it too. But the text says these Levites were "…in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things." (1 Chronicles 26:20) Treasuries, not sacrifices. Those keepers had plenty to look after, and I can barely look after one batch.

No music in this verse, friend. These fellow Levites were "…in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things." (1 Chronicles 26:20) It's a job for careful keepers.

That's right. The text says Shebuel was "…a descendant of Gershom son of Moses…" (1 Chronicles 26:24) Gershom's father is Moses. Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), so the officer over the treasuries comes from his line.
Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but he isn't the father in this verse. The text says Shebuel was "…a descendant of Gershom son of Moses…" (1 Chronicles 26:24) So Gershom's father was Moses.
Korah is the ancestor of the Korahites, who show up with the gatekeepers. But that's not who this verse names. The text says Shebuel was "…a descendant of Gershom son of Moses…" (1 Chronicles 26:24)

Yes! "They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to the repair of the house of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 26:27) Some of what they won in battle went to the house of the LORD. They took part of their winnings and gave it away. I can't even give away the last cookie without a fight in my head.
Taxes aren't mentioned here. The text says, "They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles…" (1 Chronicles 26:27) These were things from their own battles.

No harvest in this verse, friend. The text says, "They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to the repair of the house of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 26:27) The gifts came from battle plunder.

Right on, baker. "They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to the repair of the house of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 26:27) Battle winnings, and some of them went to fixing up the place. I know a thing or two about needing repairs myself, so I like that.

Plunder going to repairs sounds like a plot twist, I know. But the statement is true, so False isn't the one. The text says, "They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to the repair of the house of the LORD." (1 Chronicles 26:27) The word to catch is "some," because it wasn't all of it, just a portion set apart for fixing up the house of the LORD.

You got it! "…Chenaniah and his sons had the outside duties as officers and judges over Israel." (1 Chronicles 26:29) Outside duties, and the job titles are officers and judges. The word you picked is the second one.
No singing in this verse. The text says Chenaniah and his sons "…had the outside duties as officers and judges over Israel." (1 Chronicles 26:29) The word is judges.
Builders would be a fine job, but that's not here. The text says they were "…officers and judges over Israel." (1 Chronicles 26:29) So these were men who handled matters of the law.

Right! "In the fortieth year of David’s reign the records were searched, and strong, capable men were found among the Hebronites at Jazer in Gilead." (1 Chronicles 26:31) The records are how they were found. I bet that search felt good once it paid off. That's a lot of reading, and I would have lost my place twice.
No prophet shows up in this verse. The text says, "…the records were searched, and strong, capable men were found…" (1 Chronicles 26:31) The records did the finding.

The verse doesn't say they showed up on their own. It says, "…the records were searched, and strong, capable men were found among the Hebronites at Jazer in Gilead." (1 Chronicles 26:31) They were found through the records.

Not quite, friend. The text says King David appointed them "…for every matter pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king." (1 Chronicles 26:32) So matters of God were part of their job, right alongside the king's affairs.

That's right. King David appointed those men over the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh "…for every matter pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king." (1 Chronicles 26:32) They handled both, so the matters of God were in their care too. Both jobs, one group of men.
